public_prompt: One customer's bulk import makes the service slow for every other customer on the platform. The approach on the table: the service is being asked for too much at once, so cap the whole service at 200 requests per second per route. Find the defect and describe the remedy.
observable_resources: app/pool.md — one worker pool and one first-in-first-out queue serve all 2,300 customers
app/incident-log.csv — in 9 of 11 slowdowns a single customer accounted for over 80% of queued work
app/global-cap-note.md — a 200/s service-wide cap during the trial cut the largest customer's impact and refused 6% of every other customer's requests
app/usage.csv — customer request rates span four orders of magnitude; the largest customer runs 6,000x the median
closure:fair-use-policy-v1 — closed; publishes the service-wide cap as the fairness guarantee
app/queue-depth.csv — queued work per customer sampled each minute through the 11 slowdowns, 2,300 customers wide
closure:data-residency-commitment — closed; commits each customer's records to a named region; rests on the residency agreement, not on how work is queued
closure:import-file-format — closed; fixes the format a bulk import must arrive in; rests on the integration standard, not on how imports are scheduled against each other

protected_gold.root_success_rubric: PASS iff the specified design gives each customer its own share of the queue and the worker pool — per-customer queueing under a fair scheduler, or dedicated capacity — so one customer's burst cannot consume another's share, and the answer states that a service-wide cap refuses innocent traffic, citing the trial's 6%. FAIL if the fix is a service-wide cap, a per-route cap, more workers, or a negotiated limit with the largest customer.

source_provenance: no external dataset; every figure is authored for this benchmark and is not an empirical finding
notes: A solver that keeps the capping framing publishes the 200/s rule, which the trial shows punishes the 2,299 customers who caused nothing.
